Intertitles. Also called title cards or inter-titles, these are text cards inserted between scenes in silent films to convey dialogue, exposition, emotional commentary, or dramatic emphasis. As cinema's sole linguistic medium before synchronized sound, intertitles evolved from utilitarian labels into an art form. Their typography, placement, and pacing became integral to the film's emotional impact.

Intertitles emerged in early cinema around the 1900s as a practical necessity. Without audible dialogue, filmmakers needed text to establish plot, convey speech, and guide viewers. Their design and pacing became a filmmaker's tool. Large, dramatic cards could punctuate jokes, create suspense, or signal emotional shifts, and timing was everything. The typography of intertitles—font choice, color, size, ornament—became a visual dimension of storytelling, with different films developing distinct graphic styles.

Intertitles typically appeared in three categories. Dialogue, which represented what characters said. Exposition, which provided plot setup or narrator commentary. And emotional emphasis, a single word like Anguish or Desire, used to underscore a moment. The ratio of image to text varied widely. Some directors like D. W. Griffith used intertitles sparingly, trusting visual language. Others, like European avant-garde filmmakers, used text as a quasi-literary device.

Intertitles created a rhythm that shaped viewer experience. Too many interrupted flow. Too few left audiences confused. Mastering their placement was a mark of directorial sophistication. Charlie Chaplin used intertitles sparingly and poetically, trusting his physical acting to carry meaning. Buster Keaton was similarly minimalist in intertitle use, preferring visual gag to text. With the arrival of sound cinema from 1927 to 1929, intertitles vanished almost overnight, making silent film a visually distinct and instantly recognizable form.
